opus-5.5.text:
I think about it on a couple of different time horizons. In the near term, success looks like building an institute where scientists can actually work on the hardest, longest-horizon problems in biology without spending half their time writing grants or worrying about whether their next project is fundable. If we can give people that kind of freedom and they do things they couldn't have done anywhere else, that's a real win in itself.

But the bigger ambition is that we want to make meaningful progress on complex human diseases, the things that have resisted the usual approaches. Neurodegeneration, immune dysfunction, cancer. Those diseases are hard because they're driven by interactions across many genes, cell types, and timescales. You can't just knock out one gene in a mouse and figure it out. So part of success for us is building the tools and models that let us reason about biology at that level of complexity: better ways to perturb cells at scale, better ways to measure what happens, and increasingly, AI models that can learn from all that data and make predictions we can test.

So I'd put it this way. Success is not just publishing great papers, although we want to do that. It's whether, ten or fifteen years from now, we can point to concrete things that changed how biology gets done, and ideally to new therapeutic hypotheses or medicines that trace back to work that started here. And if we can show that a different organizational model for science actually works, one that combines curiosity-driven research with serious engineering and technology development under one roof, then other people can copy it, and that would be a huge success too.

r002.rationale: It describes success as building tools and models that enable reasoning about complex biology, including perturbation and measurement technologies that support new predictions.

r003.rationale: The response proposes a research model combining curiosity-driven science with engineering and technology development, but does not identify an Edison-style invention shop.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think about success for Arc on a couple of levels, and the honest answer is that the most important one is the hardest to measure.

The narrow version is that Arc exists to do the kind of science that's awkward to do anywhere else. Academia is extraordinary at training people and at generating ideas, but it's structurally set up around individual labs competing for individual grants on three-to-five-year cycles. Industry is great at execution once you know what you're building, but it has to answer to a product roadmap and a market. There's this gap in the middle: long-horizon, tool-building, team-based science where the payoff is a capability rather than a paper or a drug. Things like building the foundational datasets and models that let you actually ask what's going wrong in a disease, not just catalog it. If in ten years people look back and say Arc produced a handful of things that genuinely changed how biology is done, platforms that other people built on, that's success.

The broader version is about the institutional experiment itself. We're trying to show that you can give scientists real resources, no grant writing, and the ability to work in teams on problems that matter, and that this produces something different and better. If it works, I'd like the model to be copied. If other places look at Arc and say, we should fund science this way too, that's maybe the biggest win, because it compounds beyond anything our own labs would produce.

What I try hard not to use as the metric is the standard stuff: paper count, impact factor, how much press we get. Those are lagging indicators at best and actively distorting at worst. Some of the things I'm most excited about internally won't be legible to the outside world for years. So part of the job is having the discipline to hold a long time horizon and not optimize for the dashboards everyone else is looking at.

And on a personal level, I'd add that a lot of the people doing this work are early in their careers. If Arc turns out to be the place where a generation of scientists learned to think about biology as an engineering discipline, and they go on to build things we never imagined, I'd count that as success even if the institute's own name isn't on it.

astra-6.text:
I think success has to be measured by the science we enable. Are we helping people pursue important questions that they couldn’t pursue elsewhere? And does that lead to discoveries that really change how we understand biology and, ultimately, how we treat disease?

There’s also an institutional question: can we build an environment where scientists have the freedom and support to take a long-term risk, while still being rigorous about whether they’re making progress? You can’t expect every project to work. But you do want to ask whether the overall approach is producing something meaningfully different.

So I’d distinguish building an institute that’s successful from building a model that’s useful. Ideally, Arc does both: it produces great science, and it demonstrates ways of organizing and supporting research that other people can learn from.

sol-6.1.text:
I think success for Arc means enabling important science that would have been much harder to do otherwise. It’s not enough to build a new institution; the question is whether that institution helps scientists pursue ambitious ideas, develop useful tools, and make discoveries that change what we understand about biology.

There are different timescales to that. In the near term, are we attracting great people and giving them the freedom and support to do their best work? Over the longer term, does that work open up new fields or lead to better ways to treat disease? Ultimately, I’d want us to point to advances that matter and say that the way we organized and supported science helped make them possible.
